title: Self-Correction Loops
summary: Repair specific validated defects in an agent’s work through bounded feedback, preserving accepted facts and preventing repeated unsafe actions.
overview: Self-correction loops use observed errors to revise an output or proposed action. A parser error, failed test, missing citation, or tool-schema rejection can provide precise feedback. The loop is useful when the defect is repairable and a reliable validator can tell whether the repair succeeded.

Distinguish correction from retry. A transient network failure may justify repeating the same request; a malformed query needs a changed proposal; an unauthorized action must remain denied. Never allow correction prompts to weaken policy or invent missing evidence simply to satisfy a validator. Preserve original errors and accepted intermediate results.

production.poc: A prototype can feed structured validation errors back to the model once and compare repaired output with the original. Measure introduced defects as well as successful repairs.
production.production: Production classifies errors, limits attempts, protects immutable facts, and requires every revision to pass the same checks. Commands with side effects need reconciliation before any corrected attempt.
production.scale: At scale, analyze repair success by defect class and disable loops that mostly consume tokens. Frequent correction may indicate a bad schema, unclear tool contract, or inadequate base model rather than a need for more iterations.

components.name: Error classifier
components.role: Separates transient, repairable, policy-denied, and irrecoverable failures.

components.name: Validator
components.role: Produces concrete machine-readable defects and independently checks corrected artifacts.

components.name: Correction worker
components.role: Revises only the permitted fields or action arguments within the original task scope.

components.name: Protected artifact store
components.role: Retains accepted facts, previous versions, and external operation identities.

components.name: Loop governor
components.role: Caps attempts, cost, elapsed time, and repeated equivalent failures.

flow.title: Capture defect
flow.description: Record the failed artifact and a specific validator result without losing original evidence.

flow.title: Classify recoverability
flow.description: Decide whether to retry, revise, escalate, or stop based on error semantics.

flow.title: Constrain repair
flow.description: Identify editable fields and protect verified facts, permissions, and completed operations.

flow.title: Generate correction
flow.description: Request a targeted change using structured feedback and remaining budget.

flow.title: Revalidate fully
flow.description: Apply the original checks plus regression checks on previously accepted content.

flow.title: Finish or stop
flow.description: Accept the corrected artifact or return an explicit unresolved result when progress or budget is exhausted.

diagrams.caption: Only repairable defects enter correction; policy denials and uncertain effects follow different recovery paths.

useCase.title: Repairing a generated read-only query
useCase.situation: A factory analyst asks an assistant to compare downtime across production lines using a governed analytics service.
useCase.problem: The model sometimes references a renamed column or returns a query whose aggregation does not match the requested period.
useCase.requirement: The assistant must repair valid analytical mistakes without expanding access or issuing unrestricted database commands.
useCase.architecture: A read-only query gateway validates schema, permitted tables, and result shape; structured errors feed a bounded correction worker.
runtime: An unknown-column error returns the approved schema fragment, and the model proposes a corrected query within the same access scope.
The query is validated again and its result is checked for the required grouping before the explanation is generated.
useCase.failure: If the correction requests a restricted table, authorization denies it and the loop stops instead of trying alternative access paths.
useCase.impact: Track repair success, repeated error classes, introduced regressions, and total cost per accepted query. Correction is a recovery mechanism, not proof of analytical correctness.

tradeoffs.benefit: Concrete defects are often easier to fix than regenerate broadly.
tradeoffs.cost: Validators need precise and safe error messages.

tradeoffs.benefit: Some repairable tasks can recover without human work.
tradeoffs.cost: Repeated revisions consume latency and may drift from the objective.
Change constraints can limit legitimate broader corrections.

failures.scenario: The model repeats the same invalid proposal
failures.detection: Normalized artifact fingerprints and error codes repeat.
failures.recovery: Stop and escalate with the original defect evidence.

failures.scenario: A repair fixes syntax but changes the requested meaning
failures.detection: Regression checks find altered filters or aggregation semantics.
failures.recovery: Reject the revision and preserve the prior validated scope.

mistakes.mistake: Sending every failure into one repair prompt
mistakes.fix: Classify transient, semantic, policy, and uncertain-effect errors.
Keep acceptance rules stable and stop when limits are reached.

mistakes.mistake: Reexecuting a command to repair its response
mistakes.fix: Reconcile the existing operation before any new effect.

whenToUse: Defects are localized and independently detectable.
A corrected proposal can be revalidated safely.
Repair has demonstrated value within a bounded budget.
whenNotToUse: The validator cannot distinguish correct from plausible output.
The failure is an authorization denial.
The attempted effect has an unresolved external outcome.
checklist: Protect accepted facts and operation identity.
Run full regression validation after repair.
Measure repair cost and introduced errors.
